strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper extends the 'hidden knowledge' literature (Gekhman et al. 2025; Orgad et al. 2024) from binary factual correctness to distributional preference prediction, which is a genuinely new direction for interpretability methods applied to social science tasks.

Methodologically careful pipeline: the paper builds on the Geva et al. (2022) MLP decomposition with a clear derivation of how value-vector activations affect party-token logits (Eqs. 4-5), and includes a sign-inversion validation (Eq. 12) as a necessary condition for retaining value vectors, plus a layer-adaptive IQR-based selection rule.

Impressive empirical scale and breadth: 24M+ persona configurations across 7 model families (base and instruction-tuned), 6 national elections, multiple persona attributes, and 10 prompt templates per persona, with multilingual prompts (English, German, Dutch) shown in the appendix.

Evaluation design is sensible: attribute-appropriate metrics (JS for nominal, Wasserstein for ordinal attributes), survey weighting to census marginals, and party-agnostic aggregation; the finding that instruction tuning shifts predictions away from survey data, making latent estimation more valuable, is an interesting empirical insight.

Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge the first-order approximation of MLP contributions, white-box/compute requirements, and the non-uniformity of gains, and they carefully avoid overclaiming (e.g., 'complementary tool rather than a substitute for surveys').
weaknesses: No statistical uncertainty or significance testing on the central claim. Win-rates (Figs. 2, 4) and distance differences (Fig. 7) are reported as point estimates over what appears to be a modest number of attribute-party pairs per model-country cell (~8 attributes x ~5-6 parties), yet no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or paired significance tests are provided. Given that Fig. 7 medians hover near zero with wide spreads, it is hard to judge how much of the reported improvement is noise.

Missing baselines weaken the significance of the contribution. The only comparator is the model's own next-token probabilities. There is no comparison against trivial alternatives (e.g., predicting the survey marginal, party priors), against a directly trained probe/supervised predictor, or against simple ensembling of probability estimates across prompt variants—so it remains unclear whether the mechanistic machinery is what drives gains.

The entropy-gating threshold of 0.85 (Section 5.5) appears to be selected on the same data used for evaluation, a form of double-dipping. The regression analysis relating Delta_k to entropy is described only cursorily (no coefficients, no held-out validation), so the claimed 'simple gating criterion' contribution is not well supported.

Effect sizes are difficult to assess. Figures 2, 3, and 5 are dense and hard to interpret (e.g., offsets per model in Fig. 3, mixed green/red/gray semantics in Fig. 5); the text reports that gains are 'not uniform' and 'selective rather than uniform,' but the headline improvement in absolute error over probability-based estimates is never crisply quantified.

The survey ground truth measures reported voting behavior at one point in time, while prompts ask hypothetical votes; the mismatch between validated past behavior and hypothetical questions, and the fact that elections in different countries occur in different years (2019-2024), may confound cross-country comparisons that the paper attributes to context.

The contribution is a single-election-cycle, single-domain demonstration; generalization to other preference domains is asserted but not tested, and the probe training data (voting-advice applications) exist only for a handful of countries, which limits practical applicability more than the limitations section suggests.

The Impact Statement is dismissive given the sensitivity of political opinion forecasting (potential for election manipulation, demographic misrepresentation); a more substantive ethics discussion would be appropriate.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel and interesting: rather than treating an LLM's output distribution as the only signal for preference prediction, the paper identifies party-aligned MLP value vectors (building on Geva et al.'s value-vector decomposition) and aggregates persona-induced activations into distributions comparable to survey data. This bridges mechanistic interpretability and LLM-based social simulation in a way that prior hidden-knowledge work (Gekhman et al., 2025; Orgad et al., 2024), which focused on binary factual correctness, has not.

The empirical scope is impressive: ~24 million persona configurations across 7 open-weight models, 6 national elections with representative survey benchmarks, 10 prompt templates per persona, and cross-national comparison spanning multiple languages (English, German, Dutch). The data documentation (Table 1, Table 2) and release of code support reproducibility.

The paper is honestly hedged in many places: it does not claim latent estimators universally dominate, it interprets latent signals as statistical associations rather than LLM 'beliefs', and the limitations section acknowledges the first-order approximation of MLP contributions and the white-box requirement.
The entropy-based gating analysis (Section 5.5) is a useful practical contribution: it attempts to characterize *when* the latent method helps, rather than only claiming average superiority.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is only weakly supported. The abstract says mechanistic forecasting 'can improve prediction accuracy', but the evidence (Figure 7 boxplots of distance differences straddling zero; Figure 2 win-rates hovering near 50-60% with strong model/country variance; Section 5.4's own admission that gains are 'selective rather than uniform') shows effects that are small, inconsistent, and frequently negative. No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests on win-rates are reported, so it is impossible to tell whether the aggregate advantage over the probability baseline is real or noise.

The mapping from activation scores to vote distributions is ad hoc and under-validated. The paper assumes that normalized, cosine-weighted MLP activation aggregates (Eq. 13-15) are directly comparable to survey response distributions, but this monotonicity assumption is never validated independently of the end-task comparison. Because the method is only evaluated against its own weaker baseline on a single election per country, there is no out-of-sample or cross-election validation of the latent-to-preference mapping.

The probe validation is circular and its interpretability story is undermined by the paper's own evidence. Probes are trained on party position statements and evaluated on held-out splits of the same source, so the >96% F1 may reflect shallow lexical correlations rather than meaningful party representations. Table 3 (top tokens for probes and value vectors) is dominated by garbled subword fragments and mojibake, which contradicts the claim that identified value vectors encode interpretable party-aligned structure; the paper does not confront this.

The entropy gating criterion appears post hoc and circular. The threshold (>0.85) is asserted without cross-validated selection, and the regression relating Δk to entropy is estimated only on cases with Δk > 0 (Section 5.5), which selection-biases the reported relationship. A proper predictive test of the gate (e.g., pre-registered on held-out attributes/parties) is missing.

The baseline comparison may be unfair or under-tuned. The probability-based estimator is a raw next-token distribution; no strong baselines are included (e.g., ensembles of prompt templates, calibrated sampling, fine-tuned predictors), making it unclear whether latent aggregation beats simply better use of surface probabilities.

Only one election snapshot per country is used, so country-level generalization rests on a single point in time per country; combined with the acknowledged first-order approximation (ignoring layer norm, attention-mediated, and downstream interactions), the method's reliability as a forecasting tool is not established.

Presentation issues further weaken confidence: 'StemjWijzer' typo and an implausible ProDemos '2026' citation, duplicate references (von der Heyde et al. 2024a/b are the same arXiv paper), a perfunctory impact statement, and figures (e.g., Figure 2's percent-labeled win-rate axis, Figure 5's dense legend) that are hard to parse. Some key methodological details (how exactly normalized activations become probability distributions over categories) are spread across equations and remain hard to reconstruct.

strengths: Genuinely novel contribution: the paper extends 'hidden knowledge' research (Gekhman et al., 2025; Orgad et al., 2024) from binary factual correctness to distributional preference prediction, applying mechanistic interpretability (Geva et al.-style MLP value vectors) to LLM-based social simulation. This is a new and interesting angle on a well-studied problem.

Substantial empirical scale: ~24M persona configurations across 7 models (base and instruction-tuned variants of Llama 3.1, Mistral, Gemma 2, Qwen 3), 6 national elections, and multiple persona attributes, grounded in representative survey data (ANES, BES, GLES, etc.) with census-aligned weighting.

Careful methodological pipeline: linear probes on mean-pooled intermediate representations, cosine-similarity-based IQR outlier selection of value vectors, sign-inversion validation as a necessary condition for vector retention, and attribute-appropriate distance metrics (JS for nominal, Wasserstein for ordinal attributes).

The paper is appropriately hedged in places: it explicitly states gains are 'selective rather than uniform,' interprets latent signals as statistical associations rather than model beliefs, and positions the method as complementary to surveys rather than a replacement.
The entropy-based gating criterion (Section 5.5) is a practically useful idea—giving practitioners a diagnostic for when latent estimation should be preferred over output probabilities.
Honest limitations section covering white-box requirements, first-order approximation of MLP contributions, and prompt sensitivity; code is stated to be available on GitHub.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved prediction is only weakly supported. Figure 2 shows win-rates that vary widely and frequently hover near or below 50%, and the paper provides no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or sample sizes for the win-rate comparisons. With a small number of attributes/parties per model-country cell, win-rates are noisy, and the phrase 'consistently show' in Section 5.2 overstates what the figure appears to show.

The aggregation step lacks a principled calibration: mean cosine-weighted MLP activations (Eq. 14–15) are compared to survey-derived probability distributions via JS/Wasserstein distance, but no justification or validation is given for why activation magnitudes should be commensurate with probability mass. The comparison implicitly assumes a monotone, roughly linear link between activation and vote share that is never tested.

Missing baselines from interpretability: the value-vector selection machinery (probe alignment, IQR fences, sign-inversion filtering, cosine weighting) is never compared against simpler latent baselines such as directly aggregating probe logits or raw residual-stream activations. Without these, it is unclear which components of the elaborate pipeline actually drive the (modest) gains.

Evidence of possible post hoc choices: the 2.5-IQR fence, the layer range [0.5L, 0.9L], the cosine weighting, and especially the entropy threshold of 0.85 appear tuned without sensitivity analyses in the main text. The entropy gate is computed from the same output distributions being evaluated, raising circularity concerns.

Table 3 undermines the interpretability narrative: for most parties, the highest-cosine tokens for both probes and value vectors are gibberish fragments (e.g., "å¯I»", "Library", "icles"), and identical token sets appear for different parties (Liberal Democrats vs. Liberal Party of Canada; Forum voor Democratie vs. Freie Demokratische Partei). Only a handful of cases (Die Linke → 'left', Labour → 'socialist') show semantically meaningful alignment, suggesting the probe/value-vector alignment may capture shallow or confounded features rather than party semantics.

The probe F1 > 96% claim is potentially misleading: probes are trained and tested on party-statement data, but applied to persona prompts—a distribution shift whose effect on probe validity is never evaluated.

Cross-national and attribute-level findings (Section 5.4) are descriptive pattern-reading over a small number of countries; no inferential support is offered, and the claimed demographic-vs-opinion dichotomy could easily reflect the specific attribute taxonomies of the surveys used.

Presentation issues: Figure 3's offset encoding for models is hard to parse; the contribution bullet on entropy gating is interrupted by the footnote; and the claim that instruction tuning 'shifts estimations away from real-world survey predictions' rests on only a few base/instruct pairs without statistical backing.

strengths: Novel and interesting framing: the paper connects mechanistic interpretability (Geva-style MLP value-vector decomposition) to LLM-based social simulation, extending the 'hidden knowledge' literature from binary factual correctness to distributional preference prediction—a genuinely new testbed and application.

Impressive empirical scale and breadth: ~24 million persona configurations, 7 open-weight models across families and tuning regimes, 6 national elections with representative, census-weighted survey benchmarks, and 10 prompt variants per country to mitigate prompt sensitivity.

Multi-layered validation of the core mechanism: label-shuffled and random-weight controls, regression baselines, a sign-inversion necessity test (Eq. 12), a non-political intervention experiment (Fig. 9) with matched random-vector controls, and an ICL baseline that receives the same party-position data through the prompt (Fig. 10) to rule out the trivial explanation that gains come merely from external party-position data.

Methodologically careful details: attribute-appropriate distance metrics (JS for nominal, Wasserstein for ordinal), persona sampling matched to survey marginals, layer-window selection supported by an ablation (Fig. 7), and released code/prompt/probe materials supporting reproducibility.

Honest and appropriately hedged claims: the paper consistently frames gains as 'selective rather than uniform,' provides an entropy-based diagnostic for when latent forecasting helps, and includes a thoughtful impact statement discussing misuse risks (profiling, micro-targeting) and the complement-not-substitute framing for surveys.
weaknesses: Missing the most important baseline: an end-to-end linear probe trained directly on persona-induced residual representations to predict party preferences. The paper validates the value-probe direction against regression baselines for probe identification (Fig. 6), but never tests whether the elaborate value-vector selection and cosine-weighted activation aggregation actually outperforms a simple probe-based readout of the same hidden states on the forecasting task. Without this, the causal role of the value-vector machinery in the reported gains is unclear.

Evidence for the headline improvement is mixed: win-rates in Figures 2 and 4 are often near or below 50%, the ∆k distributions in Figure 11 straddle zero for most model–country pairs, and some models (e.g., Qwen3-14B, Mistral-7B-v0.1) show median differences near or below zero. The central claim that latent aggregation 'often improves' predictions rests on selective subsets rather than a robust overall gain, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the win-rate analyses in the main text.

Potential data contamination and ground-truth circularity: the elections (2019–2024) fall within or near the training windows of the evaluated models, so latent 'preference' signals may partly reflect memorized election outcomes rather than transferable knowledge of human preference structure. The paper does not discuss or test for this.

The entropy gating analysis (Section 5.5) risks post-hoc selection: the 0.85 threshold is not justified a priori, the regression on ∆k is restricted to ∆k > 0 cases (conditioning on the outcome), and the layer-window 0.5L–0.9L is selected on the same data it is evaluated on.

Presentation issues: the axes in Figures 2, 4, and 5 are largely illegible at print resolution, making it difficult for readers to verify the quantitative claims from the main-text figures alone; Figure 3's offset conventions are also hard to parse.

Scale and design confounds: Qwen3 is evaluated only at 14B while other families are 7–9B, and base-vs-instruct comparisons are uneven across families, complicating cross-model interpretation of when latent signals help.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether LLM internal representations encode preference information that is lost or distorted at the output level, extending 'hidden knowledge' research (Gekhman et al., 2025; Orgad et al., 2025) from binary factual correctness to distributional preference prediction.

The empirical scope is substantial: 7 models (base and instruction-tuned), 6 national elections across 4 languages, 280,000 persona combinations, and 10 prompt variants per country to mitigate prompt sensitivity, with real, representative election surveys as ground truth.

The paper includes a relatively thorough set of controls for its probes: label-shuffled and random-weight controls, regression baselines, a sign-inversion necessity test (Eq. 12), an intervention study in non-political contexts (Figure 9), and an in-context learning baseline that receives the same party-position data (Figure 10) to rule out that gains come simply from access to external party information.

The limitations and impact statement are honest and thoughtful: the first-order MLP approximation, per-party binary probes, white-box access requirements, and risks of population profiling are all acknowledged.
The framing of latent and surface-level signals as complementary, with an entropy-based gating criterion for when latent estimation helps, is a practically useful takeaway.
weaknesses: The headline empirical gains are weak and inconsistent. Figure 11 shows attribute-level distance differences Δk distributed around zero for nearly all model–country pairs, and win-rates in Figure 2 hover near or barely above 50% for several countries (e.g., Germany, New Zealand). The abstract's claim that mechanistic forecasting 'can improve prediction accuracy' is hedged ('sometimes more effective'), and the paper provides no significance tests or confidence intervals on whether win-rates exceed chance in the main results.

Probe F1 scores of 96–99% on held-out data are suspiciously high for such a task and are not convincingly explained. The probe training data contain party statements, responses, and explanatory comments; a plausible concern is that trivial surface features (party names, distinctive vocabulary, or tokenization artifacts) drive probe accuracy. The paper's controls (shuffled labels, random weights) rule out chance but do not rule out leakage of identifying features. Notably, Table 4 shows that most top value-vector tokens are gibberish or mojibake rather than party-related concepts, which undercuts the claim that the identified vectors 'encode party-specific representations' and suggests artifacts rather than semantic structure.

Several key methodological choices appear post-hoc or weakly justified: the 2.5-IQR cosine-similarity fence, the 0.5L–0.9L layer window ('highest lower whisker' is a fragile selection criterion), the cosine weighting in Eq. (13), and especially the entropy gate of 0.85 in Section 5.5, which is applied selectively ('we selectively evaluate... only for attributes with normalized entropy exceeding 0.85') and risks circularity: the condition under which mechanistic forecasting is declared successful is itself defined via LLM output statistics, not validated out of sample.

The evaluation benchmark is survey data rather than actual election outcomes, and since the persona distribution is sampled to match survey marginals, the comparison measures agreement with one survey instrument. More importantly, the paper never compares against the obvious practical alternative: a simple supervised model trained directly on the survey data to predict party shares from persona attributes. Without such a baseline, it is unclear what the latent pipeline adds over existing survey methodology, weakening the significance claim.

The aggregated activation score (Eq. 14) is a heuristic average of cosine-weighted activations with no principled justification or ablation in the main text for why this specific aggregation should track preference distributions; alternatives (e.g., softmax over aggregate activations, diametric-vector handling) are not systematically compared.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Figures 2, 4, and 5 have small, rotated, hard-to-read axis labels; key quantitative results (median improvements, exact win-rates) are described only qualitatively in the text; and the main text relies heavily on appendix figures for the actual evidence.

The connection between the mechanistic analysis and the forecasting result is loose: the paper shows the identified vectors causally influence party-token logits (Figures 8–9), but the forecasting gains could arise from generic linear readouts of intermediate layers rather than the specific 'value vector' decomposition; the regression baselines in Figure 6 partially address this but are evaluated only on probe classification, not on downstream forecasting performance.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel direction: applying mechanistic interpretability (MLP value-vector probing à la Geva et al.) to preference prediction rather than binary factual correctness, extending the 'hidden knowledge' line of work (Gekhman et al., 2025; Orgad et al., 2025) to inherently distributional, contextual outcomes.

The empirical scale is impressive and well beyond comparable persona-simulation studies: 7 model families (base and instruction-tuned), 6 national elections from representative surveys, 280,000 persona combinations, 10 hand-crafted and native-speaker-verified prompt templates per country, and over 24 million configurations.

The methodological pipeline is carefully validated: label-shuffled and random-weight controls, regression baselines, sign-inversion (local necessity) tests, a non-political intervention control (Figure 9), an in-context learning baseline that controls for the external party-position data (Figure 10), and a layer-window ablation (Figure 7). This is more rigorous than typical probing papers.

The framing of findings is honest and appropriately hedged: the authors consistently report that gains are 'selective rather than uniform,' distinguish demographic from opinion-based attributes, and derive an interpretable entropy-gating criterion for when latent estimation helps.

Reproducibility is strong: probe datasets, prompt templates, and code are released; the limitations and impact statements are thoughtful and candid (first-order approximation, white-box requirement, misuse risks).
weaknesses: The headline win-rate results (Figures 2, 4) are presented descriptively without confidence intervals or formal significance tests on whether latent estimation systematically outperforms probability-based estimation. Figure 11 shows Δk distributions straddling zero for most model-country pairs, so the aggregate claim that mechanistic forecasting 'improves prediction accuracy' rests on win-rate proportions whose uncertainty is not quantified.

Probe F1 scores exceeding 96% are suspiciously high and raise the concern that probes capture superficial, token-level party markers (e.g., party names in the shuffled-party-list) rather than deep party structure; near-perfect generalization from voting-advice statements to persona prompts would be remarkable and warrants more scrutiny of potential leakage from the probe prompt templates.

The effect sizes are modest and the practical significance is not fully established: the paper never evaluates against actual election outcomes, only against (weighted) survey distributions, and the median absolute errors in Figures 3 and 5 remain large (often 10-30 percentage points), so neither method produces usable forecasts in an absolute sense.

The entropy-gating threshold of 0.85 appears post hoc and its selection is not justified or validated out-of-sample; the regression relating Δk to entropy is only described at a high level, and evaluating the gate only on cases with Δk > 0 risks circularity.

The probability-based baseline may be under-powered: it is pure next-token probability aggregation, whereas the latent method benefits from explicit calibration against party-position data; stronger surface-level baselines (e.g., logit ensembling, prompt ensembling with the same party-position data) are only partially covered by the ICL baseline.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: several figures (e.g., Figures 2 and 5) have illegible axis labels and dense layouts; key quantitative details (probe dimensions, number of selected value vectors per party, normalization details in Eq. 13) are relegated or unspecified in the main text.
